question: For a vehicle requiring a Class A or B CDL, when is a tank endorsement required to haul a liquid or liquid gas?
choice_a: When the tank or tanks have an individual rated capacity of more than 119 gallons and an aggregate rated capacity of 1,000 gallons or more
choice_b: Only when the liquid being hauled is classified as a hazardous material
choice_c: Only when the tank is permanently welded to the vehicle frame
choice_d: Whenever the vehicle has three or more axles
explanation: The manual states a tank endorsement is required for a Class A or B vehicle hauling liquid or liquid gas in a tank or tanks with an individual rated capacity of more than 119 gallons and an aggregate rated capacity of 1,000 gallons or more, whether permanently or temporarily attached.
source_note: New Mexico CDL Manual, Section 8 - Tank Vehicles, This Section Covers

question: Does the liquid or gas being hauled have to be a hazardous material for the Class A/B tank endorsement requirement to apply?
choice_a: Yes, only DOT-classified hazardous liquids trigger the requirement
choice_b: No, the liquid or gas does not have to be a hazardous material
choice_c: Only if the liquid is flammable
choice_d: Only if the tank capacity exceeds 5,000 gallons
explanation: The manual specifically notes that the liquid or gas does not have to be a hazardous material for the tank endorsement requirement to apply to Class A or B vehicles.
source_note: New Mexico CDL Manual, Section 8 - Tank Vehicles, This Section Covers

question: When is a tank endorsement required for a driver operating a Class C vehicle?
choice_a: Class C vehicles are always exempt from the tank endorsement requirement
choice_b: Only when hauling drinking water for human consumption
choice_c: When the vehicle is used to transport hazardous materials in liquid or gas form in tanks of the capacities described for Class A/B vehicles
choice_d: Only when driven outside New Mexico
explanation: The manual states a tank endorsement is also required for Class C vehicles when used to transport hazardous materials in liquid or gas form in tanks of the above-described rated capacities.
source_note: New Mexico CDL Manual, Section 8 - Tank Vehicles, This Section Covers

question: Why should a driver inspect a tanker before loading, unloading, or driving it?
choice_a: To calculate the resale value of the vehicle
choice_b: It is only necessary after a reported accident
choice_c: To satisfy an annual paperwork requirement only
choice_d: To make sure the vehicle is safe to carry the liquid or gas and safe to drive
explanation: The manual states that inspecting a tanker before loading, unloading, or driving makes sure the vehicle is safe to carry the liquid or gas and is safe to drive.
source_note: New Mexico CDL Manual, Section 8 - Tank Vehicles, This Section Covers

question: On all tank vehicles, what is the most important item to check for during inspection?
choice_a: Leaks, checking under and around the vehicle
explanation: The manual states that on all tank vehicles, the most important item to check for is leaks, checking under and around the vehicle for signs of any leaking.
source_note: New Mexico CDL Manual, Section 8 - Tank Vehicles, 8.1.1 Leaks

question: According to the manual, what happens if a driver carries liquids or gases in a leaking tank?
choice_a: It is permitted if the driver notes it on the trip log
choice_b: It is a crime; the driver will be cited, prevented from driving further, and may be liable for spill clean-up
choice_c: The driver receives a warning only for a first offense
choice_d: It is allowed as long as the leak is below the waterline of the tank
explanation: The manual states that carrying liquids or gases in a leaking tank is a crime, and the driver will be cited, prevented from driving further, and may also be liable for clean-up of any spill.
source_note: New Mexico CDL Manual, Section 8 - Tank Vehicles, 8.1.1 Leaks

question: What must a driver check regarding the intake, discharge, and cut-off valves on a tank vehicle?
choice_a: That they are removed before highway driving
choice_b: That they are lubricated weekly regardless of use
choice_c: That the valves are in the correct position before loading, unloading, or moving the vehicle
choice_d: That they are painted a bright color for visibility
explanation: The manual instructs drivers to check the intake, discharge, and cut-off valves and make sure the valves are in the correct position before loading, unloading, or moving the vehicle.
source_note: New Mexico CDL Manual, Section 8 - Tank Vehicles, 8.1.1 Leaks

question: What should a driver check about manhole covers and vents on a tank vehicle?
choice_a: That the covers are removed for ventilation during transport
choice_b: That the vents are taped shut to prevent spills
choice_c: That the covers are replaced with clear panels for visual inspection
choice_d: That the covers have gaskets and close correctly, and that the vents are kept clear so they work correctly
explanation: The manual instructs drivers to check manhole covers and vents, making sure the covers have gaskets and close correctly, and to keep the vents clear so they work correctly.
source_note: New Mexico CDL Manual, Section 8 - Tank Vehicles, 8.1.1 Leaks

topic: Inspecting Tank Vehicles - Special Purpose Equipment
question: Which items does the manual list as special purpose equipment to check on a tank vehicle, if so equipped?
choice_a: Vapor recovery kits, grounding and bonding cables, emergency shut-off systems, and a built-in fire extinguisher
choice_d: Auxiliary cab heater and sleeper berth curtains
explanation: The manual lists vapor recovery kits, grounding and bonding cables, emergency shut-off systems, and a built-in fire extinguisher as special purpose equipment to check on tank vehicles, if so equipped.
source_note: New Mexico CDL Manual, Section 8 - Tank Vehicles, 8.1.2 Check Special Purpose Equipment

question: Under what circumstance does the manual say a driver should never drive a tank vehicle?
choice_a: With a full load of fuel in the saddle tanks
choice_b: With open valves or manhole covers
choice_c: With the cab dome light on
explanation: The manual warns that a driver should never drive a tank vehicle with open valves or manhole covers.
source_note: New Mexico CDL Manual, Section 8 - Tank Vehicles, 8.1.2 Check Special Purpose Equipment

question: Why does the manual say hauling liquids in tanks requires special driving skills?
choice_a: Because tank vehicles are not equipped with mirrors
choice_b: Because tank vehicles cannot be equipped with air brakes
choice_c: Because of the high center of gravity and liquid movement
choice_d: Because tank vehicles are lighter than flatbed trailers
explanation: The manual states that hauling liquids in tanks requires special skills because of the high center of gravity and liquid movement.
source_note: New Mexico CDL Manual, Section 8 - Tank Vehicles, 8.2 Driving Tank Vehicles

question: What does the manual mean by a tank vehicle's 'high center of gravity,' and why is it dangerous?
choice_a: The vehicle sits low to the ground, making it prone to hydroplaning
choice_b: The load is concentrated at the rear axle, making steering difficult
choice_c: The load shifts side to side only when the tank is empty
choice_d: Much of the load's weight is carried high up off the road, making the vehicle top-heavy and easy to roll over
explanation: The manual explains that high center of gravity means much of the load's weight is carried high up off the road, making the vehicle top-heavy and easy to roll over, and that liquid tankers are especially easy to roll over.
source_note: New Mexico CDL Manual, Section 8 - Tank Vehicles, 8.2.1 High Center of Gravity

question: According to the manual, how should a tank vehicle driver take highway curves and on-ramp/off-ramp curves?
choice_a: Well below the posted speed, since tests have shown tankers can turn over at the speed limits posted for curves
choice_b: At exactly the posted speed limit
choice_c: Slightly above the posted speed to maintain momentum through the curve
choice_d: Speed is not a factor as long as the tank is baffled
explanation: The manual states that tests have shown tankers can turn over at the speed limits posted for curves, so drivers should take highway curves and on-ramp/off-ramp curves well below the posted speeds.
source_note: New Mexico CDL Manual, Section 8 - Tank Vehicles, 8.2.1 High Center of Gravity

question: What does the manual identify as the cause of liquid surge in a tank vehicle?
choice_a: The tank being loaded completely full with no empty space
choice_b: Movement of the liquid in partially filled tanks
choice_c: Cold temperatures causing the liquid to contract
choice_d: The presence of bulkheads dividing the tank
explanation: The manual states that liquid surge results from movement of the liquid in partially filled tanks, which can have bad effects on handling.
source_note: New Mexico CDL Manual, Section 8 - Tank Vehicles, 8.2.2 Danger of Surge

question: What can happen when a tank vehicle comes to a stop and the liquid surges toward the end of the tank?
choice_a: The surge only reduces fuel economy, with no effect on handling
choice_b: The surge automatically engages the trailer's emergency brakes
choice_c: The wave can push the truck in the direction it is moving, and on a slippery surface can shove a stopped truck out into an intersection
choice_d: The surge has no effect unless the tank is baffled
explanation: The manual explains that when the wave hits the end of the tank it tends to push the truck in the direction the wave is moving, and on a slippery surface such as ice this can shove a stopped truck out into an intersection.
source_note: New Mexico CDL Manual, Section 8 - Tank Vehicles, 8.2.2 Danger of Surge

question: What are bulkheads in a liquid tank, and what must a driver pay attention to when loading or unloading tanks that use them?
choice_a: External braces that prevent rollover entirely, requiring no special attention
choice_b: Devices that eliminate the need to check for outage
choice_c: Panels that convert part of the tank into a refrigerated compartment
choice_d: Dividers that create several smaller tanks; the driver must pay attention to weight distribution, not putting too much weight on the front or rear of the vehicle
explanation: The manual states that some liquid tanks are divided into several smaller tanks by bulkheads, and when loading and unloading these smaller tanks, the driver must pay attention to weight distribution, not putting too much weight on the front or rear of the vehicle.
source_note: New Mexico CDL Manual, Section 8 - Tank Vehicles, 8.2.3 Bulkheads

question: How do baffled liquid tanks help control surge, and what surge problem can still occur?
choice_a: Baffles are bulkheads with holes that let liquid flow through, helping control forward-and-backward surge, but side-to-side surge can still occur and can cause a rollover
choice_b: Baffles eliminate all surge in every direction, making rollover impossible
choice_c: Baffles are used only in tanks hauling dry bulk goods, not liquids
choice_d: Baffles increase forward-and-backward surge to help braking performance
explanation: The manual states baffled tanks have bulkheads with holes that let liquid flow through, which helps control forward and backward surge, but notes side-to-side surge can still occur and can cause a rollover.
source_note: New Mexico CDL Manual, Section 8 - Tank Vehicles, 8.2.4 Baffled Tanks

question: What does the manual say un-baffled ('smooth bore') tanks are usually used to haul, and why?
choice_a: Explosives, because baffles could create dangerous friction
choice_b: Food products such as milk, because sanitation regulations forbid the use of baffles due to the difficulty of cleaning the inside of the tank
choice_c: Dry bulk cement, because baffles are unnecessary for solid cargo
choice_d: Compressed gases, because baffles would trap gas pockets
explanation: The manual states that un-baffled tankers, sometimes called smooth bore tanks, are usually those that transport food products such as milk, since sanitation regulations forbid the use of baffles because of the difficulty in cleaning the inside of the tank.
source_note: New Mexico CDL Manual, Section 8 - Tank Vehicles, 8.2.5 Un-baffled Tanks
